actuarial.headline: 2025 Variance Prize honors research comparing credibility theory and machine learning for ratemaking
actuarial.summary: The CAS awarded its 2025 Variance Prize ($5,000) to "Adjusting Manual Rates to Own Experience: Comparing the Credibility Approach to Machine Learning" by Christophe Dutang, Giorgio Alfredo Spedicato, and Quentin Guibert. The paper contrasts classical credibility theory against modern machine learning and transfer-learning methods for the core P&C ratemaking problem of adjusting manual (class) rates to an individual risk's own experience -- the same experience-rating problem underlying workers' comp and commercial GL/auto pricing. The authors show the two approaches are complementary rather than substitutes, with ML able to supplement but not replace credibility-based judgment in practice. The Editor-in-Chief specifically framed the result as showing how classical and modern techniques "can work together to improve ratemaking," giving pricing actuaries a concrete basis for blending the two in commercial lines rate filings.

actuarial.headline: CAS releases second edition of its AI Primer, adding agentic AI guidance and an AI-driven reserving workflow
actuarial.summary: The Casualty Actuarial Society published the second edition of "The CAS AI Primer: Practical Guidance for Actuaries" on July 27, 2026, maintained by the CAS Artificial Intelligence Working Group on a quarterly review cycle. New in this edition: a section on agentic AI covering its operational mechanics, workflow integration, adoption frameworks and risks; updated descriptions of current AI models' actuarial capabilities; and a visual walkthrough of an AI-driven claims reserving process. The primer's throughline is responsible use -- validation, governance, and retained professional judgment -- rather than wholesale automation. It targets P&C actuaries at all AI-experience levels rather than one specific line, so treat this as cross-cutting governance guidance rather than a line-specific development.

actuarial.headline: M6.8 earthquake strikes Kumamoto, Japan, damaging commercial and industrial property
actuarial.summary: A magnitude 6.8 earthquake (initially reported as 7.1, revised by USGS) struck south of Kumamoto city at roughly 10km depth on July 28, 2026, registering Shindo 7 -- the top of the Japanese intensity scale -- in the worst-hit areas. Reported damage includes a collapsed section of an Aeon shopping mall with people trapped, damage to the Nippon Paper Industries Yatsushiro plant with workers reported missing, expressway and industrial-structure damage, and roughly 48,000 households without power. For context, the 2016 Kumamoto quake (M7.0) generated up to $4 billion in insurance/reinsurance losses, and there is currently $1.55 billion of outstanding cat bond limit exposed to Japanese quake risk, though most of that capacity is indemnity- or parametric-triggered against residential rather than commercial exposure, meaning the corporate and industrial losses reported here will likely fall more heavily on traditional commercial property and reinsurance treaties than on the cat bond market.

actuarial.headline: Munich Re Specialty launches parametric earthquake cover for corporates in Japan via Lloyd's
actuarial.summary: Munich Re Specialty launched a parametric earthquake insurance product for corporate clients in Japan, distributed through the Lloyd's Japan platform and structurally supported by Munich Re's Capital Partners division. The trigger uses seismic-intensity readings from Japan's Kik-net and K-NET monitoring station networks rather than a physical damage assessment, so payouts can be released quickly to fund business continuity and operational recovery after a quake. It is aimed broadly at Japanese businesses seeking protection beyond traditional indemnity-based property cover, closing a protection gap for corporates that need fast liquidity rather than a lengthy claims-adjustment process. No policy limits, pricing, or initial take-up figures were disclosed at launch (July 28, 2026).

data_science.headline: Bloomberg open-sources Causal-TS, a unified library for causal discovery in high-dimensional, nonstationary time series
data_science.summary: Bloomberg researcher Mohammad Fesanghary released Causal-TS, an open-source Python library (pip-installable, Python 3.10-3.12) implementing four specialized causal-discovery algorithms -- CDNOTS, CDNOTS+, CEDAR, and GRACE -- plus wrappers for established methods (GES, Granger, LASSO-VAR, LGES), all sharing one GPU-accelerated conditional-independence test layer via PyTorch. A regime-discovery pipeline detects structural breaks with pluggable changepoint detectors and reruns discovery with regime-specific parameters, and optional DoWhy integration takes the pipeline from raw multivariate series to causal effect estimates. This directly targets the practical problem of causal structure that shifts over time -- relevant to any actuarial time series work (claims trends, mortality, macro drivers) where the causal structure isn't assumed stationary. Code is available at github.com/bloomberg/causal-ts.

data_science.headline: New regret-optimal algorithm for non-stationary dynamic pricing closes a long-standing theoretical gap
data_science.summary: Jiang and Zhao study contextual dynamic pricing where demand follows a generalized linear model (GLM) whose true parameters can change over time in an unknown way, and propose a multiscale change-point-detection algorithm that adapts without needing to know the number of stationary segments or the magnitude of parameter drift in advance. The method achieves regret of order O(sqrt(s_T*d*T) AND {V_T^(1/3)*d^(1/3)*T^(2/3) + sqrt(d*T)}), where s_T counts piecewise-stationary segments and V_T is a newly defined design-adjusted variation budget -- and the authors prove a matching minimax lower bound, confirming optimality up to log factors. They note existing adaptive non-stationary bandit methods don't transfer to this setting because contexts vary across arrivals, so this closes a genuine gap rather than incrementally tuning an existing method. For actuarial pricing teams running GLM-based rating engines with periodic re-calibration, this gives a principled, adaptive alternative to fixed-window refits when the underlying demand or loss relationship drifts.

data_science.headline: Systematic study finds distributional (non-mean) splitting mostly doesn't beat CART for random forests -- except on multivariate responses
data_science.summary: Koemen implements four distributional random-forest split criteria (isotropic and anisotropic random-Fourier-feature MMD, adaptive-frequency MMD, and a sliced-Wasserstein criterion, plus post-hoc kernel-mean shrinkage) inside one honest-forest codebase and benchmarks them against standard mean-based CART splitting across synthetic quantile mechanisms, real univariate datasets, a California-housing curve, and multivariate synthetic/real responses. The finding actuaries should note: on ordinary scalar tabular regression, plain CART remains the robust default and frequently wins outright, and the fancier distributional-splitting variants don't systematically beat isotropic MMD. Distributional splitting only earns its keep on multivariate responses with genuine non-location (dependence) structure -- e.g., a copula example where the energy score separates methods even though marginal CRPS does not. All criteria and the paired-comparison harness ship in the open-source, Rust-backed `drforest` library. This is a useful corrective for reserving/pricing teams tempted to adopt more exotic tree-splitting criteria for tabular claims data: the added complexity mostly isn't justified unless the target is genuinely multivariate.

data_science.headline: Meta's proxymate framework diagnoses and corrects bias in proxy-outcome inference -- a direct analogue to loss-development risk in reserving
data_science.summary: Darmon, Sinha, Wilkins-Reeves and Gocmen present proxymate, an open-source framework for validating and correcting inference that relies on proxy outcomes -- short-term signals, model predictions, or surrogate endpoints used in place of a primary outcome that is too slow to mature, too rare, or too hard to measure directly. The framework checks four distinct failure levels -- population representativity, unit-level measurement quality, estimate-level decision validity, and cross-domain transportability -- each paired with targeted adjustment strategies rather than a single blanket correction. At Meta, the tool has been applied across experimentation, prevalence estimation, and monitoring use cases and has "assessed and corrected millions of proxy/primary comparisons," enabling faster decisions on thousands of experiments where naive proxy-based confidence intervals would have been miscalibrated. The structural problem -- inference from an immature signal standing in for a slow-to-mature true outcome -- is exactly the loss-development problem in reserving (early paid/incurred data as a proxy for ultimate losses), making the diagnostic taxonomy a useful lens even though the paper itself has no insurance application.

data_science.headline: Generative crowdsourcing model jointly models item difficulty and class-dependent annotator skill to recover rare labels
data_science.summary: Singer, Gruffaz, Vo Van and Vayatis address class-imbalanced crowdsourced labeling, where annotators can be uniformly reliable, uniformly unreliable, or specialists on just the majority or minority class -- and where the minority label is usually the operationally important one (e.g., a rare defect or fraud flag). Prior label-aggregation models capture either class-dependent annotator error or item difficulty, but not both together; this paper introduces a generative model combining both, revisits Condorcet's Jury Theorem under class imbalance, and proves majority voting asymptotically preserves the true class proportion. Evaluated across 33 real-world crowdsourcing datasets (images and text, spanning both many-annotations-per-item and many-items regimes), the model consistently achieves the best minority-class recall while staying competitive on balanced accuracy. This is directly transferable to insurance rare-event labeling problems -- claims-fraud flagging, SIU referral triage, underwriting red-flag review -- where multiple reviewers disagree and the rare positive class is what actually matters.

data_science.headline: Consolidated best-practices guide for building large-scale ML-derived maps from Earth observation data
data_science.summary: Sialelli, Young, Jiang, Aybar and co-authors present a condensed, end-to-end best-practices guide for turning satellite Earth-observation data into operational, large-scale ML-derived maps, organized around six coupled stages: EO data infrastructure, data selection/preprocessing, ML dataset construction and training, uncertainty quantification, map production/distribution, and independent validation. The paper's central warning is that design choices made early (preprocessing, dataset construction) quietly propagate errors into the final map, and that uncertainty quantification and independent validation are the two stages most often under-resourced relative to their importance. While framed generically, this is directly applicable to catastrophe and climate-risk modeling teams that increasingly build exposure and peril maps (flood, wildfire, wind) from ML on satellite imagery, where the same validation and error-propagation risks apply to the resulting commercial-property risk scores. A longer companion guide with full methodological depth is linked from the paper.
